lines.text: Carbohydrates and fats keep a body running. Neither one builds it.
Consider what a body has to do besides move. A six-year-old grows into a sixteen-year-old.
A cut on your hand closes over in a week. Hair grows, nails grow, muscle thickens with
training. All of that is construction work, and construction needs material.
Proteins are used to build new tissue and repair damaged tissue. This is why the diet of a
growing child must contain enough protein, and why an athlete training for strength needs
more than a person who is not. A body short of protein cannot grow properly, however
much energy it is given — you cannot build a wall out of firewood.
Plant sources of protein include all pulses — moong, tuar dal, gram, kidney beans, peas —
along with soya bean, groundnut and other nuts and seeds. Animal sources include milk,
curd, paneer, cheese, egg, fish, chicken and meat. Edible mushrooms are a good source too.
Because of the job they do, protein-rich foods are called body-building foods — while
carbohydrates and fats, which supply energy, are together called energy-giving foods.
Which foods in your Table 3.1 diary were body-building foods?
Did every day of the week contain at least one?
Mushrooms Mushrooms are not plants. They belong to a separate group of
living things — fungi — and they grow in dark, damp places without sunlight.
Edible mushrooms are a good source Of protein, which is unusual for a
food that is neither a pulse nor an animal product.
